classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a translated exponential and a line on the same axes, then rearrange the equation and use the relative positions and shapes of the graphs to justify exactly two solutions.

answer.short: The blue curve is $y=e^x$ shifted down $3$ units. Its $y$-intercept is $(0,-2)$ and its horizontal asymptote is $y=-3$.
answer.worked:
Shift $y=e^x$ down $3$ units. The horizontal asymptote moves to $y=-3$.

$$\begin{align*}y&=e^0-3\\y&=-2\end{align*}$$

The curve passes through $(0,-2)$ and rises from left to right.

children.label: b
children.prompt: On the same set of axes, sketch $y=x$.

answer.short: The red line $y=x$ passes through the origin and has gradient $1$.
answer.worked: On the same axes, draw the straight line through $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. Its gradient is $1$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use your diagram to explain why $e^x-x-3=0$ has exactly two real solutions.

answer.short: Exactly two real solutions. The graphs of $y=e^x-3$ and $y=x$ intersect twice.
answer.worked: The equation $e^x-x-3=0$ is equivalent to $e^x-3=x$. Its solutions are the $x$-coordinates of the intersections. The sketch shows one intersection to the left of the $y$-axis and one to the right. The exponential curve bends strictly upwards, so it can meet a straight line at most twice.

spec.description: One set of axes with the blue translated exponential, red line, black intersection dots and y-axis ticks at −2 and −3. Each curve has arrows at both ends.
spec.mathematics: y = e^x − 3 and y = x intersect once near (−2.95,−2.95) and once near (1.51,1.51). The exponential crosses the y-axis at −2 and tends to y = −3 on the left.
